entries.test: Public demonstrations of Deep Research and Galactica would establish whether both generate science-sounding articles on user-selected topics.
entries.note: “Remake” is a functional comparison, not a claim of shared code or technical lineage.

entries.test: Published usage figures and independent adoption studies would establish whether Deep Research achieves substantial use.
entries.note: “We can be sure” expresses a firm prediction without a deadline.

entries.test: Public investigations available by publication would show whether LLM-generated junk content had measurably degraded online information or search results.
entries.note: The claim asserts partial confirmation, not complete vindication of the earlier conjecture.

entries.test: Public studies tracing increased online junk content to Deep Research's speed and expanded generation capabilities would test the claimed worsening and mechanism.
entries.note: The statement explicitly attributes worsening pollution to the tool's capabilities; it also predicts a future outcome.

entries.test: Documented cases of scammers using Deep Research to produce unreliable medical reports on advertising-supported websites would establish the predicted use.
entries.note: The commercial use can be documented publicly without requiring access to an unexpressed private motive.
“May” makes the comparative prediction explicitly a possibility.
“Not so great” supplies an assessment of quality without specifying a factual defect.

entries.test: Public evaluations of AI systems available at publication would establish their factual accuracy and reliability in information synthesis and multistep research.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion identifies hallucinations and incorrect inferences as the relevant failures.

entries.test: Representative user studies pairing initial credibility judgments with expert accuracy checks would show whether virtually all outputs appear legitimate, including erroneous ones.
entries.note: Superficial credibility and actual accuracy can be measured separately.

entries.test: Public behavioral studies measuring careful fact-checking and testing the effect of polished presentation would establish whether apparent quality discourages verification.
entries.note: “Since” explicitly supplies a causal explanation for the predicted behavior.

entries.test: Public grading studies or documented classroom outcomes would show whether Deep Research-written term papers consistently receive A grades and students quickly recognize this.
entries.note: The normalization drops “every” and “quickly.” Despite its exaggerated wording, the original makes a testable prediction about grades.

entries.test: Published author disclosures and audits of scientific papers would establish researcher use of Deep Research and resulting errors that escaped detection during publication.
entries.note: Errors initially missed can later be identified by public audits.

entries.test: Public correction, retraction, and citation records would show whether identified Deep Research errors persist in the scientific literature after entering it.
entries.note: The antecedent is entry of the errors into the literature. The normalization broadens Deep Research errors to AI-introduced errors generally.

entries.test: Public training-data disclosures and model evaluations would establish whether later models ingest Deep Research output and suffer degradation attributable to that training.
entries.note: The preceding model-collapse discussion supports the normalization's reference to degradation.

entries.test: Public audits identifying erroneous Deep Research material incorporated into scientific publications would establish contamination of the literature.
entries.note: In context, “infected” means incorporation of erroneous generated material.

entries.test: Public investigations of paper mills and journal submission records would show whether Deep Research drives a large production increase, overwhelms review, and spreads errors difficult to detect and correct.
entries.note: The original predicts actual expansion, whereas “will let” describes enablement. The normalization also omits difficulty detecting the errors.

entries.test: Public audits and documented consequences would show whether Deep Research produces a large influx of unreliable medical content that causes substantial problems.
entries.note: “When—not if” firmly predicts the influx. The surrounding discussion supplies a plain reading involving unreliable medical information.
